what_it_does: When programmers declare a variable as a 32-bit integer, the compiler on a small embedded device (the kind that runs on a battery-powered sensor or microcontroller) faithfully uses 32 bits for every operation on that variable — even when the actual value at runtime fits in 8 or 16 bits. This wastes energy, because wider arithmetic and bigger memory transfers consume more power. BitSpec is a combined compiler-and-hardware approach that bets on values being small: the compiler shrinks variable representations to the narrowed width it expects will be sufficient and generates cheap narrow instructions. Tiny hardware monitors watch the live values; if a value ever overflows the narrowed representation (the bet was wrong), the hardware signals a 'misspeculation' and software re-runs that computation at the original safe width. In the common case where the bet is right, the program runs with less energy; correctness is always preserved by the fallback.
